This tutorial fits a connected pySEB structure to three real SANS datasets.
The sample is a water-in-cyclohexane microemulsion stabilized by an Aerosol
OT (AOT) surfactant layer. Isotopic substitution highlights the water core,
the complete droplet, or the surfactant shell while leaving the underlying
geometry unchanged.

The measurements are official
[SasData example data](https://www.sasview.org/docs/old_docs/6.1.0/user/example_data/testdata_help.html)
collected on the LOQ instrument at ISIS. The
[SasView simultaneous-fitting tutorial](https://www.sasview.org/downloads/simultaneous_1d_fitting_in_sasview_v6.pdf)
documents the sample, contrasts, scattering-length densities, and a more
complete analysis.

This is a baseline fit, not a publication-ready analysis. The model below is
monodisperse and unsmeared. The final residuals deliberately show why real SAS
analysis must test those assumptions.

## What you will fit

The structure contains two linked subunits:

```text
SolidSphere core.center = shell.center SolidSphericalShell

core radius = R
shell inner radius = R
shell outer radius = R + thickness
```

The three datasets share the core radius, shell thickness, and droplet volume
fraction. Their known contrasts change `beta_core` and `beta_shell`, and each
measurement receives its own flat background.

## Install the fitting dependency

Continue in the environment used for the introductory tutorials and add
SciPy:

```bash
python -m pip install scipy
```

pySEB evaluates the scattering structure. SciPy's
[`least_squares`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.least_squares.html)
adjusts bounded parameters to minimize the uncertainty-weighted residuals.

## 1. Load the measured data

The CSV files contain q in Å⁻¹, intensity in cm⁻¹, and the measured intensity
uncertainty. They are three-column extracts of the upstream CanSAS XML files;
no intensities have been synthesized or altered.

- [Core contrast data](data/aot-core-contrast.csv){download="aot-core-contrast.csv"}
- [Drop contrast data](data/aot-drop-contrast.csv){download="aot-drop-contrast.csv"}
- [Shell contrast data](data/aot-shell-contrast.csv){download="aot-shell-contrast.csv"}
- [SasData BSD-3-Clause license](data/SASDATA-LICENSE.txt){download="SASDATA-LICENSE.txt"}

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pyseb
import sympy
from numpy.polynomial.hermite import hermgauss
from scipy.optimize import least_squares
from scipy.special import ndtr, ndtri


data_directory = Path("data")
data_files = {
    "Core": data_directory / "aot-core-contrast.csv",
    "Drop": data_directory / "aot-drop-contrast.csv",
    "Shell": data_directory / "aot-shell-contrast.csv",
}

datasets = {}
for name, path in data_files.items():
    q, intensity, uncertainty = np.loadtxt(
        path, delimiter=",", skiprows=3, unpack=True
    )
    datasets[name] = {
        "q": q,
        "intensity": intensity,
        "uncertainty": uncertainty,
    }

print({name: data["q"].size for name, data in datasets.items()})
```

Each original dataset has 137 points. We use q ≤ 0.25 Å⁻¹ and require a
positive uncertainty. This removes the final high-q points where intensities
fluctuate around zero and one reported uncertainty is zero.

```{python}
for name, data in datasets.items():
    selected = (data["q"] <= 0.25) & (data["uncertainty"] > 0)
    for key in ("q", "intensity", "uncertainty"):
        data[key] = data[key][selected]

print({name: data["q"].size for name, data in datasets.items()})
```

## 2. Build the two-subunit structure

The shell and core are connected through their fixed `center` references.
Setting the shell's inner radius equal to the core radius makes the two
subunits occupy adjacent, non-overlapping volumes.

```{python}
world = pyseb.World("AOTMicroemulsionFit")
droplet = world.Add("SolidSphere", "core")
world.Link(
    "SolidSphericalShell",
    "shell.center",
    "core.center",
)
world.Add(droplet, "droplet")
```

Unlike a single preassembled core–shell function, this is an explicit pySEB
structure. Its total amplitude and core–shell interference follow from the
link between two reusable subunits.

### Inspect the generated form factor

`World.FormFactor()` returns the normalized symbolic expression assembled by
pySEB. Printing it here makes the equation being fitted inspectable rather
than hiding it behind the numerical evaluator.

```{python}
form_factor_expression = pyseb.SymPyExpression(
    str(world.FormFactor("droplet"))
).expr

print("Normalized pySEB form factor P(q) =")
print(form_factor_expression)
```

The printed expression is easier to read in factored form. Define
$x_c=qR$, $x_i=qR_i$, and $x_o=qR_o$:

$$
A_c(q)=3\frac{\sin(x_c)-x_c\cos(x_c)}{x_c^3},
$$

$$
A_s(q)=3\frac{x_i\cos(x_i)-x_o\cos(x_o)-\sin(x_i)+\sin(x_o)}
{x_o^3-x_i^3}.
$$

The normalized form factor generated by the linked structure is

$$
P(q)=\left[
\frac{\beta_c A_c(q)+\beta_s A_s(q)}{\beta_c+\beta_s}
\right]^2.
$$

Consequently, the unnormalized quantity used for the absolute-intensity fit
is

$$
I_{pySEB}(q)=(\beta_c+\beta_s)^2P(q)
             =[\beta_cA_c(q)+\beta_sA_s(q)]^2.
$$

::: {.callout-note title="Why use spheres here?"}
The source analysis treats these AOT droplets as spherical core–shell
particles, so a sphere is the parsimonious starting hypothesis. It has one
size coordinate, and pySEB provides an exact non-overlapping
`SolidSphere`–`SolidSphericalShell` construction.

A spheroid would introduce at least an equatorial radius, a polar radius, and
their associated distributions. More importantly, pySEB currently provides a
homogeneous `Spheroid` but no solid spheroidal-shell subunit. Simply linking
two homogeneous spheroids at their centers would create overlapping volumes
and would not by itself define a rigid, aligned core–shell spheroid. Testing
anisotropy properly therefore requires a `SolidSpheroidalShell` model (or an
equivalent aligned composite) followed by a fit-quality comparison that
justifies its extra parameters.
:::

## 3. Convert contrast into excess scattering length

The SLD values below are in units of 10⁻⁶ Å⁻² and are fixed from the SasView
tutorial. Each tuple contains core, shell, and solvent SLD.

```{python}
sld = {
    "Core": (6.39, 0.62, -0.28),
    "Drop": (-0.55, 0.62, 6.68),
    "Shell": (6.39, 0.62, 6.68),
}
```

For a homogeneous region, its excess scattering length is
$\beta=(\rho-\rho_{solvent})V$. The measured dilute-particle intensity is

$$
I(q)=\frac{\phi}{V_{total}} I_{pySEB}(q)10^8 + B,
$$

where $\phi$ is volume fraction, $I_{pySEB}$ is the unnormalized form factor
in Å², $10^8$ converts Å⁻¹ to cm⁻¹, and $B$ is a flat background.

```{python}
def calculate_intensity(
    contrast,
    q,
    core_radius,
    shell_thickness,
    volume_fraction,
    background,
):
    outer_radius = core_radius + shell_thickness
    core_volume = 4.0 * np.pi * core_radius**3 / 3.0
    total_volume = 4.0 * np.pi * outer_radius**3 / 3.0
    shell_volume = total_volume - core_volume

    core_sld, shell_sld, solvent_sld = sld[contrast]
    parameters = {
        "R_core": core_radius,
        "Ri_shell": core_radius,
        "Ro_shell": outer_radius,
        "beta_core": (
            (core_sld - solvent_sld) * 1e-6 * core_volume
        ),
        "beta_shell": (
            (shell_sld - solvent_sld) * 1e-6 * shell_volume
        ),
    }

    unnormalized = np.asarray(
        world.EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized(
            "droplet", parameters, q.tolist()
        )
    )
    return (
        volume_fraction / total_volume * unnormalized * 1e8
        + background
    )
```

The signed betas are important. In core contrast, the shell is close to the
solvent match point, so the core dominates. In shell contrast, the core is
close to the solvent match point, so the shell dominates. Drop contrast
retains substantial scattering from both regions.

## 4. Define one simultaneous residual vector

The optimizer sees six independent fit parameters:

1. shared core radius;
2. shared shell thickness;
3. shared volume fraction;
4. core-contrast background;
5. drop-contrast background;
6. shell-contrast background.

::: {.callout-note title="This is already a multivariable fit"}
The radius, thickness, and volume fraction move together during optimization;
they are not fitted one at a time. The three backgrounds also move, giving six
fitted variables in total. Sharing the first three variables across all three
contrasts is what makes this a simultaneous fit.
:::

Every residual is divided by its measured uncertainty, so a value of two
means the calculation misses that point by two reported standard deviations.

```{python}
contrast_order = ("Core", "Drop", "Shell")


def residual_vector(values):
    core_radius, shell_thickness, volume_fraction = values[:3]
    backgrounds = values[3:]
    residuals = []

    for contrast, background in zip(contrast_order, backgrounds):
        data = datasets[contrast]
        prediction = calculate_intensity(
            contrast,
            data["q"],
            core_radius,
            shell_thickness,
            volume_fraction,
            background,
        )
        residuals.append(
            (prediction - data["intensity"]) / data["uncertainty"]
        )

    return np.concatenate(residuals)
```

## 5. Fit with physically useful bounds

The initial values are deliberately approximate. Bounds prevent negative
sizes, volume fractions, and backgrounds while still leaving a broad search
region.

```{python}
initial = np.array([20.0, 10.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1])
lower = np.array([5.0, 1.0, 0.001, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
upper = np.array([60.0, 30.0, 0.2, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0])

fit = least_squares(
    residual_vector,
    initial,
    bounds=(lower, upper),
    x_scale="jac",
)

parameter_names = (
    "core radius (Å)",
    "shell thickness (Å)",
    "volume fraction",
    "core background (cm^-1)",
    "drop background (cm^-1)",
    "shell background (cm^-1)",
)
for name, value in zip(parameter_names, fit.x):
    print(f"{name:28s} {value:.6g}")

degrees_of_freedom = fit.fun.size - fit.x.size
reduced_chi_squared = np.sum(fit.fun**2) / degrees_of_freedom
print(f"reduced chi-squared         {reduced_chi_squared:.3f}")
```

The shared geometry is close to a 25 Å water core with an 8 Å surfactant
layer. The fitted volume fraction is close to 0.056. These are plausible
values, but the large reduced chi-squared warns that plausible parameters do
not by themselves establish an adequate model.

## 6. Plot data, fit, and normalized residuals

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-aot-simultaneous-fit
#| fig-cap: "Simultaneous baseline fit of the linked sphere-and-shell structure to three AOT microemulsion contrasts."

core_radius, shell_thickness, volume_fraction = fit.x[:3]
backgrounds = fit.x[3:]

figure, axes = plt.subplots(
    3, 2, figsize=(10, 10), sharex="col",
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.55, 1.0]},
)

for row, (contrast, background) in enumerate(
    zip(contrast_order, backgrounds)
):
    data = datasets[contrast]
    prediction = calculate_intensity(
        contrast,
        data["q"],
        core_radius,
        shell_thickness,
        volume_fraction,
        background,
    )
    normalized_residual = (
        data["intensity"] - prediction
    ) / data["uncertainty"]

    positive = data["intensity"] > 0
    axes[row, 0].errorbar(
        data["q"][positive],
        data["intensity"][positive],
        yerr=data["uncertainty"][positive],
        fmt=".",
        markersize=3,
        label="measurement",
    )
    axes[row, 0].plot(data["q"], prediction, label="pySEB fit")
    axes[row, 0].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_yscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"{contrast}\n$I(q)$ (cm$^{{-1}}$)")
    axes[row, 0].legend(fontsize="small")

    axes[row, 1].plot(data["q"], normalized_residual, ".", markersize=3)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(0.0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].axhline(-2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 1].set_ylabel("residual / uncertainty")

axes[-1, 0].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
axes[-1, 1].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Random residuals scattered mostly between -2 and +2 would support the model.
Instead, long runs of positive and negative residuals remain, especially for
drop and shell contrast. The optimizer converged; the physical model is what
needs improvement.

## 7. Improve the model with size distributions

The baseline assumes that every droplet has exactly the same core radius and
shell thickness. Real microemulsions contain a distribution of sizes. We now
fit two more shared variables:

7. relative standard deviation of the core radius;
8. relative standard deviation of the shell thickness.

The core radius uses a positive log-normal distribution. The shell thickness
uses a normal distribution truncated at zero, because a negative thickness is
not physical. Both are number distributions: each sampled droplet contributes
according to its probability, and the absolute intensity uses the population's
mean total volume.

Evaluating dozens of sizes through the high-level pySEB API on every optimizer
step would be unnecessarily slow. Instead, ask pySEB for the structure's
symbolic form factor once and compile that expression into a NumPy function.
The fitted equation still comes from the same two-subunit pySEB graph.

```{python}
normalized_expression = form_factor_expression

(
    q_symbol,
    core_radius_symbol,
    shell_inner_symbol,
    shell_outer_symbol,
    beta_core_symbol,
    beta_shell_symbol,
) = sympy.symbols(
    "q R_core Ri_shell Ro_shell beta_core beta_shell"
)

unnormalized_expression = normalized_expression * (
    beta_core_symbol + beta_shell_symbol
) ** 2
evaluate_form_factor = sympy.lambdify(
    (
        q_symbol,
        core_radius_symbol,
        shell_inner_symbol,
        shell_outer_symbol,
        beta_core_symbol,
        beta_shell_symbol,
    ),
    unnormalized_expression,
    modules="numpy",
)
```

Seven-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature represents the log-normal core
distribution. Eleven equal-probability samples represent the positive part of
the shell-thickness distribution. These small deterministic grids make the
tutorial reproducible and quick; a publication analysis should verify that
increasing the number of samples no longer changes the result.

```{python}
hermite_nodes, hermite_weights = hermgauss(7)
normal_weights = hermite_weights / np.sqrt(np.pi)
shell_quantiles = (np.arange(11) + 0.5) / 11


def lognormal_samples(mean, relative_sd):
    sigma_log = np.sqrt(np.log1p(relative_sd**2))
    values = mean * np.exp(
        np.sqrt(2) * sigma_log * hermite_nodes
        - 0.5 * sigma_log**2
    )
    return values, normal_weights


def positive_normal_samples(center, relative_sd):
    lower_probability = ndtr(-1.0 / relative_sd)
    probabilities = lower_probability + (
        1.0 - lower_probability
    ) * shell_quantiles
    values = center * (
        1.0 + relative_sd * ndtri(probabilities)
    )
    weights = np.full(shell_quantiles.size, 1.0 / shell_quantiles.size)
    return values, weights
```

For each contrast, average the unnormalized intensity over all sampled core
radii and shell thicknesses before applying volume fraction and background.

```{python}
def calculate_disperse_intensity(
    contrast,
    q,
    core_radius,
    shell_thickness,
    core_relative_sd,
    shell_relative_sd,
    volume_fraction,
    background,
):
    core_values, core_weights = lognormal_samples(
        core_radius, core_relative_sd
    )
    shell_values, shell_weights = positive_normal_samples(
        shell_thickness, shell_relative_sd
    )
    core_sld, shell_sld, solvent_sld = sld[contrast]

    averaged_intensity = np.zeros_like(q)
    mean_total_volume = 0.0

    for radius, radius_weight in zip(core_values, core_weights):
        for thickness, thickness_weight in zip(
            shell_values, shell_weights
        ):
            sample_weight = radius_weight * thickness_weight
            outer_radius = radius + thickness
            core_volume = 4.0 * np.pi * radius**3 / 3.0
            total_volume = 4.0 * np.pi * outer_radius**3 / 3.0
            shell_volume = total_volume - core_volume
            beta_core = (
                (core_sld - solvent_sld) * 1e-6 * core_volume
            )
            beta_shell = (
                (shell_sld - solvent_sld) * 1e-6 * shell_volume
            )

            sample_intensity = np.asarray(
                evaluate_form_factor(
                    q,
                    radius,
                    radius,
                    outer_radius,
                    beta_core,
                    beta_shell,
                )
            )
            averaged_intensity += sample_weight * sample_intensity
            mean_total_volume += sample_weight * total_volume

    return (
        volume_fraction / mean_total_volume
        * averaged_intensity
        * 1e8
        + background
    )
```

Fit the eight variables simultaneously. The initial geometry, volume fraction,
and backgrounds come from the monodisperse fit; only the two distribution
widths are new guesses.

```{python}
def disperse_residual_vector(values):
    (
        core_radius,
        shell_thickness,
        core_relative_sd,
        shell_relative_sd,
        volume_fraction,
    ) = values[:5]
    residuals = []

    for contrast, background in zip(contrast_order, values[5:]):
        data = datasets[contrast]
        prediction = calculate_disperse_intensity(
            contrast,
            data["q"],
            core_radius,
            shell_thickness,
            core_relative_sd,
            shell_relative_sd,
            volume_fraction,
            background,
        )
        residuals.append(
            (prediction - data["intensity"]) / data["uncertainty"]
        )

    return np.concatenate(residuals)


disperse_initial = np.concatenate(
    (fit.x[:2], [0.12, 0.42], fit.x[2:])
)
disperse_lower = np.array(
    [5.0, 1.0, 0.01, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
)
disperse_upper = np.array(
    [60.0, 30.0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.2, 5.0, 5.0, 5.0]
)

disperse_fit = least_squares(
    disperse_residual_vector,
    disperse_initial,
    bounds=(disperse_lower, disperse_upper),
    x_scale="jac",
)

disperse_parameter_names = (
    "core radius (Å)",
    "shell thickness (Å)",
    "core relative SD",
    "shell relative SD",
    "volume fraction",
    "core background (cm^-1)",
    "drop background (cm^-1)",
    "shell background (cm^-1)",
)
for name, value in zip(disperse_parameter_names, disperse_fit.x):
    print(f"{name:28s} {value:.6g}")

disperse_degrees_of_freedom = (
    disperse_fit.fun.size - disperse_fit.x.size
)
disperse_reduced_chi_squared = (
    np.sum(disperse_fit.fun**2) / disperse_degrees_of_freedom
)
print(f"baseline reduced chi-squared {reduced_chi_squared:.3f}")
print(
    "disperse reduced chi-squared "
    f"{disperse_reduced_chi_squared:.3f}"
)
```

| Quantity | Monodisperse fit | Size-distribution fit | SasView tutorial |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Core radius | 24.75 Å | 23.74 Å | about 23.5 Å |
| Shell thickness | 8.29 Å | 6.93 Å | about 7.3 Å |
| Core relative SD | — | 0.105 | about 0.12 |
| Shell relative SD | — | 0.503 | about 0.42 |
| Reduced chi-squared | 29.50 | 20.30 | not reported |

The fitted distribution widths are genuine optimizer variables, not values
copied from the [SasView tutorial](https://www.sasview.org/downloads/simultaneous_1d_fitting_in_sasview_v6.pdf).
Their proximity to that independent analysis is a useful check, not proof that
the model is complete.

## 8. Compare the improved fit

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-aot-disperse-fit
#| fig-cap: "Adding fitted core-radius and shell-thickness distributions improves all three contrasts. The dashed line is the monodisperse baseline."

(
    core_radius,
    shell_thickness,
    core_relative_sd,
    shell_relative_sd,
    volume_fraction,
) = disperse_fit.x[:5]
backgrounds = disperse_fit.x[5:]

figure, axes = plt.subplots(
    3, 2, figsize=(10, 10), sharex="col",
    gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.55, 1.0]},
)

for row, (contrast, background) in enumerate(
    zip(contrast_order, backgrounds)
):
    data = datasets[contrast]
    prediction = calculate_disperse_intensity(
        contrast,
        data["q"],
        core_radius,
        shell_thickness,
        core_relative_sd,
        shell_relative_sd,
        volume_fraction,
        background,
    )
    baseline_prediction = calculate_intensity(
        contrast,
        data["q"],
        fit.x[0],
        fit.x[1],
        fit.x[2],
        fit.x[3 + row],
    )
    normalized_residual = (
        data["intensity"] - prediction
    ) / data["uncertainty"]

    positive = data["intensity"] > 0
    axes[row, 0].errorbar(
        data["q"][positive],
        data["intensity"][positive],
        yerr=data["uncertainty"][positive],
        fmt=".",
        markersize=3,
        label="measurement",
    )
    axes[row, 0].plot(
        data["q"], baseline_prediction,
        color="grey", linestyle="--", label="monodisperse",
    )
    axes[row, 0].plot(
        data["q"], prediction, label="with size distributions"
    )
    axes[row, 0].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_yscale("log")
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(f"{contrast}\n$I(q)$ (cm$^{{-1}}$)")
    axes[row, 0].legend(fontsize="small")

    axes[row, 1].plot(data["q"], normalized_residual, ".", markersize=3)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(0.0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    axes[row, 1].axhline(2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].axhline(-2.0, color="grey", linewidth=0.6, linestyle="--")
    axes[row, 1].set_xscale("log")
    axes[row, 1].set_ylabel("residual / uncertainty")

axes[-1, 0].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
axes[-1, 1].set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The extra variables reduce the systematic mismatch and bring the geometry
close to the more complete SasView analysis. They do not make the residuals
random or reduce the reduced chi-squared to approximately one. The official
analysis also applies an approximate 10% $dQ/Q$ LOQ resolution smearing
correction and still describes its result as imperfect.

This is the useful stopping point for an introductory fit: the improvement is
visible and statistically measurable, but the tutorial does not disguise the
remaining model error. Optimization answers “what parameters best satisfy
this model?” Residual analysis asks the more important question, “is this
model adequate for the experiment?”

## What this demonstrates

- A fit can use an explicit linked pySEB structure rather than a single
  preassembled subunit.
- Contrast variation changes signed scattering weights while sharing the same
  structure geometry.
- `EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized` connects subunit betas to absolute-scale
  intensity.
- The generated symbolic form factor can be compiled once for efficient
  averaging over fitted size distributions.
- Simultaneous residuals enforce shared physical parameters across datasets.
- A successful optimizer and plausible parameters do not guarantee a good
  scattering model.
